nodes.name: Dual nitrogen precursor polymerization
nodes.procedure: Aniline and CM were first dissolved in 1.5M HCl solution, followed by the addition of iron (III) chloride as the iron precursor and ammonium persulfate as oxidant for the oxidative PANI polymerization. The solution was stirred at room temperature for ~4 hours to allow full polymerization of aniline.

nodes.description: ORR RRDE testing in acidic electrolyte
nodes.source_text: Rotating ring-disk electrode (RRDE) testing in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ revealed a half-wave potential of 0.80 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), with a well-defined mass transport-limited current density (Fig. 2A). Ring-current values from RRDE measurements verified that the H₂O₂ yield remained < 2.5% at all electrode potentials. This low H₂O₂ yield corresponds to an average electron-transfer number per O₂ molecule (n_e) of >3.95. The catalyst performance loss after 30,000 RDE potential cycles was ~5% (fig. S3).

nodes.description: H₂-air fuel cell performance at 35 wt% Nafion
nodes.source_text: Performance of (CM+PANI)-Fe-C cathode catalyst layers (CCLs) in the membrane electrode assembly (MEA) was investigated under realistic conditions for the cathode operated on air (Fig. 2B). The maximum power density reached with an electrode containing 35 weight % (wt % Nafion ionomer was 0.39 W cm⁻² at 1.0 bar partial pressure of H₂ and air... The current density of ~75 mA cm⁻² at a reference voltage of 0.8 V [~90 mA cm⁻², iR corrected (i, current; R, resistance), fig. S4A]

nodes.description: H₂-air fuel cell performance at increased air flow
nodes.source_text: These results are corroborated by an improvement in fuel cell performance of the (CM+PANI)-Fe-C cathode with 35 wt% Nafion when the air flow was increased from 200 to 760 standard cubic centimeters per minute (Fig. 2C). Higher current densities were observed across the entire range of investigated voltages, including an increase in maximum power density from 0.39 to 0.42 W cm⁻²

By comparison, also shown in Fig. 2B is the performance of a 10 wt% Pt/C cathode (0.1 mgPt cm⁻²) prepared by a decal transfer method. Under identical test conditions, nearly the same current densities as those measured for (CM+PANI)-Fe-C catalyst were obtained in the kinetic region (>0.75 V).

nodes.description: H₂-O₂ fuel cell performance at different O₂ pressures
nodes.source_text: Experiments under H₂-O₂ conditions were also performed... Three different partial pressures of O₂ - 0.3, 1.0, and 2.0 bar-were applied... The maximum power density values of ~0.87 and 0.94 W cm⁻² reached at pO₂ of 1.0 and 2.0 bar, respectively, were the highest ever achieved with PGM-free ORR catalysts operating on oxygen.

nodes.description: H₂-air fuel cell performance at 50 wt% Nafion ionomer
nodes.source_text: Electrodes with increased ionomer content (50 and 60 wt % Nafion) were also fabricated and exhibited enhanced current densities at fuel cell voltages >0.7 V resulting from more effective filling and lining of macropores by the ionomer that improved catalyst utilization.

nodes.description: H₂-air fuel cell performance at 60 wt% Nafion ionomer
nodes.source_text: Electrodes with increased ionomer content (50 and 60 wt % Nafion) were also fabricated and exhibited enhanced current densities at fuel cell voltages >0.7 V... However, the performance improvement at low current densities came at the expense of hindered water removal, manifesting itself as a performance decrease in the mass transport region (below 0.6 V).

nodes.characterization_summary: BET surface area of ~1500 m²/g achieved for (CM+PANI)-Fe-C catalyst.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After completion of the (CM + PANI) -Fe-C catalyst synthesis, a surface area of ~1500 m² g⁻¹ was achieved, as determined by the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method.

nodes.characterization_summary: Mesopore volume ~0.25 cm³/g and micropore volume ~0.61 cm³/g for (CM+PANI)-Fe-C catalyst.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The volumes of mesopores (pore diameter 2 to 50 nm) and micropores (pore diameter < 2 nm), as measured with nitrogen adsorption measurements, were ~0.25 and ~0.61 cm³ g⁻¹, respectively (Fig. 1A).

nodes.characterization_summary: BET surface area of only ~1000 m²/g for PANI-Fe-C catalyst.
nodes.evidence_snippet: PANI-Fe-C, i.e., the catalyst obtained without using CM as a pore former, was much more aggregated (Fig. 1B) than the combined (CM + PANI)-Fe-C catalyst (Fig. 1C), which contained fewer pores with diameter >50 nm and a BET surface area of only ~1000 m² g⁻¹.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM images show PANI-Fe-C more aggregated than (CM+PANI)-Fe-C with fewer large pores.
nodes.evidence_snippet: (B and C) SEM images of PANI-Fe-C and (CM+PANI)-Fe-C catalysts, respectively, demonstrating the effect of CM in macropore formation.

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM reveals macropores providing accessibility to active sites and improved ionomer distribution in (CM+PANI)-Fe-C electrode.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The vital role of macropores in providing greater accessibility to the catalytically active sites and establishing a more open framework for improving the ionomer distribution within catalyst layers was revealed by high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF)-STEM imaging of a microtomed cross section of a (CM + PANI) Fe-C catalyst electrode (fig. S2, A and B).

nodes.characterization_summary: Fluorine EDX mapping shows ionomer impregnates macroporous regions but not dense regions of (CM+PANI)-Fe-C electrode.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure S2B shows a fluorine energy-dispersive x-ray (EDX) spectroscopy elemental map acquired from the same area shown in fig. S2A.

nodes.characterization_summary: AC-STEM reveals fibrous carbon particles, few-layer graphene sheets, and single Fe atoms primarily at graphitic basal-plane edges in (CM+PANI)-Fe-C catalyst.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Atomic-level images of FeN₄ active sites were obtained with low-voltage (60 kV), aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM).

nodes.characterization_summary: EELS with single-atom resolution confirms FeN₄ structures embedded within carbon basal planes; N 3.5 at% and Fe 0.2 at% in both carbon phases; average Fe:N ratio consistent with FeN₄.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) with single-atom resolution confirmed such FeN₄ structures embedded within carbon basal planes. These two carbon phases each contained similar amounts of N [3.5 atomic % (at %)] and Fe (0.2 at %), as determined by EELS.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS shows N 5.0 at% and Fe 0.3 at% near surface; N1s peak indicates pyridinic-, pyrrolic-, and graphitic-nitrogen species.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The nitrogen and iron contents within the near-surface regions of the catalyst measured by x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were 5.0 and 0.3 at %, respectively... Analysis of the XPS N1s peak indicated the presence of pyridinic-, pyrrolic-, and graphitic-nitrogen bonded species (fig. S5).

nodes.characterization_summary: Raman I_D/I_G ratio of 1.07 confirms abundance of graphitic (002) basal-plane edges.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Raman spectra for (CM + PANI)-Fe-C (fig.S7) confirmed an abundance of the (002) basal-plane edges as verified by a high D band-to-G band intensity ratio (I_D / I_G 1.07).

nodes.characterization_summary: Broad (002) peak indicates very small graphitic domain size with turbostratic alignment.
nodes.evidence_snippet: A broad (002) peak in the x-ray diffraction pattern (fig.S8) also indicated a very small graphitic domain size coupled with turbostratic alignment of the basal planes within the domains.
